Measuring progress, well-being and beyond GDP

Search for a keyword(s) or time series ID

Gross domestic product (GDP) measures the value of goods and services produced in the UK. It estimates the size of the economy and its growth.

Contact: Email Gross Domestic Product team

Real Time Indicators: Look Ahead to September 2026

In the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026:

Real gross domestic product (GDP) grew by 0.7%, following growths of 0.5% in the three months to July 2026 and a growth of 0.5% in the three months to June 2026 (both July and June are revised up from a 0.4% growth in our previous publication).

Services output grew by 0.9%, after growing by 0.7% in the three months to July 2026 (revised up from a 0.6% growth in our previous publication).

Production output fell by 0.2%, following a fall of 0.7% in the three months to July 2026 (revised down from a fall of 0.5% in our previous publication).

Construction output fell by 1.0%; this follows a fall of 0.2% in the three months to July 2026 (revised up from a fall of 0.5% in our previous publication).

Monthly GDP grew by 0.1% in August 2026, following an unrevised growth of 0.4% in July 2026 and a growth of 0.4% in June 2026 (revised up from a 0.3% growth in our previous publication).

The growth in August was driven by a 0.8% growth in production, with services showing no growth, and construction falling by 0.2% in August 2026.

This release is consistent with the quarterly national accounts release published on 30 September 2026, which itself is consistent with Blue Book 2026.

Real gross domestic product (GDP) is estimated to have grown by 0.7% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026. This is the eighth consecutive three-month on three-month growth and follows growths of 0.5% in both the three months to July 2026 and in the three months to June 2026 (both July and June are revised up from 0.4% growths in our previous publication). The largest contribution to the three-month on three-month growth came from the services sector, which grew by 0.9% in the three months to August 2026. There were falls in the remaining two main sectors, with a fall of 1.0% in construction sector and a 0.2% fall in the production sector in August 2026. This release includes revisions to July 2026 estimates for the first time. It also incorporates revisions from January 1997 to June 2026 estimates, in line with our quarterly national accounts published on 30 September 2026. July 2026 revisions are the result of updated source data; revisions prior to July are covered in the quarterly national accounts release. These revisions are consistent with Blue Book 2026. More information can be found in Section 7: Revisions to GDP .  Note that early estimates of GDP are subject to revision in future publications (both positive and negative) as more data become available and we subsequently update for that additional information. Please see our Why GDP figures are revised article for more information on revisions, and our recent blog on managing the trade-off between timeliness and accuracy when producing GDP.

Monthly real GDP is estimated to have grown by 0.1% in August 2026, following a growth of 0.4% in July 2026 (unrevised from our previous publication), and a growth of 0.4% in June 2026 (revised up from a 0.3% growth in our previous publication). Production grew by 0.8%, services showed no growth and construction fell by 0.2% in August 2026.

Figure 2: Real GDP is estimated to have grown by 1.8% in the three months to August 2026 compared with the same three months a year ago

Source: Gross domestic product (GDP) monthly estimate from the Office for National Statistics

Download this chart Figure 2: Real GDP is estimated to have grown by 1.8% in the three months to August 2026 compared with the same three months a year ago

Looking over the longer term, GDP is estimated to have grown by 1.8% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the same three months a year ago. Over this period, services grew by 2.2%, production grew by 0.8%, while construction fell by 1.6%. This was last higher in the three months to October 2022, compared with the previous year, when it grew by 2.0%. Compared with the same month a year ago, GDP is estimated to be 2.1% higher in August 2026. This was last higher in August 2022 when it grew by 2.6% compared with the same month a year ago. The sectors with the largest positive contributions to growth in the three months to August 2026, compared with a year ago are professional, scientific and technical activities, and information and communication. Within these sectors, the industries with the largest positive contributions are:

computer programming, consultancy and related activities (contributing 0.32 percentage points to GDP)

legal activities (contributing 0.22 percentage points)

scientific research and development (contributing 0.18 percentage points)

advertising and market research (contributing 0.11 percentage points)

information service activities (contributing 0.10 percentage points to GDP)

Combined, these industries contribute 0.93 percentage points to the 1.8% GDP growth, and 1.15 percentage points to the 2.2% growth in services in the three months to August 2026 compared to the same period a year ago.

Services output grew 0.9% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026, and was the only positive contributor to the growth seen in gross domestic product (GDP) in the three months to August 2026. This follows a growth of 0.7% in the three months to July 2026 (revised up from 0.6% in our previous publication), and a growth of 0.6% in the three months to June 2026 (revised up from 0.5% in our previous publication). Figure 3: Services output grew by 0.9% in the three months to August 2026, following a growth of 0.7% in the three months to July 2026 Monthly index and three-month on three-month growth rates for the services sector, UK, January 2024 to August 2026

The embedded visualisation below may not display correctly without JavaScript enabled. View it in full screen .

There was a rise in output in 10 of the 14 subsectors in the three months to August 2026, with the largest positive contributions at the subsector level coming from:

professional, scientific and technical activities (up 2.8%), driven by growths in accounting, bookkeeping and auditing activities; tax consultancy (up 5.5%), scientific research and development (up 4.9%), and legal activities (up 3.4%)

information and communication (up 2.8%), which was mainly driven by a growth of 5.0% in computer programming, consultancy and related activities. At an industry level, computer programming, consultancy and related activities has been the industry with the largest contribution to three-monthly growth in each of the last sixth months.

administrative and support service activities (up 3.0%), driven by growths of 7.6% in rental and leasing activities and 5.9% in services to buildings and landscape activities

The largest negative contributions at the subsector level came from wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (down 0.1%), driven by a fall of 2.3% in wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles, contributing a 0.08 percentage point fall to top level GDP. This marked four consecutive three-month on three-month falls (Figure 5). Weakness in this industry came from Wholesale on a fee or contract basis and other specialised wholesale (excl. wholesale of solid, liquid and gaseous fuels and related products).

On the month, services output showed no growth in August 2026. This follows growths of 0.5% in July 2026 (revised up from a growth of 0.4% in our previous publication), and 0.5% in June 2026 (revised up from a growth of 0.4% in our previous publication). In August 2026, 4 of the 14 subsectors grew. The largest positive contribution came from wholesale and retail trade; repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles, which grew by 2.0% in August 2026. This was mainly driven by a growth of 3.8% in wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles, which contributed 0.16 percentage points to services output and 0.13 percentage points to real GDP in July 2026. (Figure 5). This growth follows five consecutive month-on-month falls and remains 1.6% lower than February 2026. The main contributor to monthly growth was wholesale of information and communication equipment. This coincides with a period of recent strength within computer programming, consultancy and related activities.

Figure 5: Wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles, fell by 2.3% in the three months to August, but grew by 3.8% in the month to August 2026

Monthly index of wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles, UK, January 2024 to August 2026

Download this chart Figure 5: Wholesale trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles, fell by 2.3% in the three months to August, but grew by 3.8% in the month to August 2026

The second largest positive contribution to services sector output in August 2026 came from professional, scientific and technical activities (up 1.5%). This was driven by growths in legal activities (up 3.3%), architectural and engineering activities; technical testing and analysis (up 2.0%), and advertising and market research (up 2.6%). The largest negative contribution to services output in August 2026 was administrative and support service activities (down 1.7%). This was driven by falls in rental and leasing activities (down 2.4%), office administrative, office support and other business support activities (down 2.2%), and employment activities (down 1.4%). Consumer-facing services Consumer-facing services output grew by 0.4% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026. The largest positive contributions in this period came from:

retail trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles (up 1.1%)

wholesale and retail trade and repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles (up 1.9%)

The largest negative contributions in this period came from:

food and beverage service activities (down 1.5%)

buying and selling, renting and operating of own or leased real estate, excluding imputed rent (down 0.5%)

travel agency, tour operator and other reservation service and related activities (down 1.7%)

Figure 6: Consumer-facing services grew by 0.4% in the three months to August 2026, with the largest positive contribution coming from retail trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles

Download this chart Figure 6: Consumer-facing services grew by 0.4% in the three months to August 2026, with the largest positive contribution coming from retail trade, except of motor vehicles and motorcycles

Consumer-facing services fell by 0.3% in August 2026, following a fall of 0.1% in July 2026 (revised up from a fall of 0.4% in our previous publication), and a growth of 0.4% in June 2026 (unrevised from our previous publication). The largest negative contribution at the industry level came from sports activities and amusement and recreation activities (down 7.1%). This follows a fall of 1.2% in July 2026 (revised down from a 0.3% fall in our previous publication). Food and beverage service activities was the second largest negative contributor, with a fall of 2.7%. The largest positive contribution to consumer-facing services in August 2026 came from wholesale and retail trade and repair of motor vehicles and motorcycles, which grew by 2.7%. Our Monthly Business Survey (MBS) is used for 44.3% of the services sector by industry weight. The turnover response rate for the MBS element of the services sector was 88.7% in August 2026, which is broadly as expected at this point in the data reporting cycle. We would expect this to increase over time as more responses are received. Any new data will be included in future monthly GDP releases. For context, the average turnover response rate for the service sector in 2024 and 2025 now stands at 97.6%, and 97.9%, respectively.  More detailed breakdowns on services are available in our Index of Services, UK: August 2026 release .

The production sector is estimated to have fallen by 0.2% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026. This follows revised falls of 0.7% in the three months to July 2026 (revised down from a fall of 0.5% in our previous publication) and 0.1% in the three months to June 2026 (revised down from no growth in our previous publication). Figure 7: Production output fell by 0.2% in the three months to August 2026, despite growing by 0.8% in the month of August 2026 Monthly index and three-month on three-month growth rates for index of production, UK, January 2024 to August 2026

The embedded visualisation below may not display correctly without JavaScript enabled. View it in full screen .

In the three months to August 2026, the production sector fell by 0.2%, with negative contributions coming from water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (down 3.1%), and mining and quarrying (down 0.6%). These falls were partially offset by growths in manufacturing (up 0.1%), and electricity, gas, steam and air conditioning supply (up 0.4%). Figure 8: Production sectors monthly indices and three-monthly growth rates Monthly index and three-month on three-month growth rates for the production sectors, UK, January 2024 to August 2026

The embedded visualisation below may not display correctly without JavaScript enabled. View it in full screen .

On the month, the production output is estimated to have grown by 0.8% in August 2026, this follows a rise of 0.3% in July 2026 (revised up from 0.2% in our previous publication), and a fall of 0.2% in June 2026 (unrevised from our previous publication). This was driven by growths in manufacturing (up 1.2%), mining and quarrying (up 1.4%) and electricity, gas steam and air conditioning supply (up 0.1%). These growths were partially offset by a fall in water supply; sewerage, waste management and remediation activities (down 1.2%) Manufacturing output Manufacturing output grew by 0.1% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026, with 7 of the 13 subsectors increasing over this period. The largest positive contributions came from:

manufacturing of computer, electronic and optical products (up 3.5%)

manufacture of machinery and equipment n.e.c. (up 1.8%)

These growths were partially offset by falls elsewhere, with the largest negative contributions coming from:

manufacture of basic metals and metal products (down 2.7%)

manufacture of rubber and plastics products, and other non-metallic mineral products (down 2.5%)

manufacture of wood and paper products, and printing (down 1.6%)

Figure 9 shows both the three-month and monthly contributions to manufacturing output from each of the manufacturing sub-sectors.

Download this chart Figure 9: Manufacture of computer, electronic and optical products was the largest contributor to the 0.1% growth in manufacturing output in the three months to August 2026

In the month of August 2026, manufacturing output grew by 1.2%, with 9 of the 13 subsectors seeing growth. This follows a growth of 1.0% in July 2026 (revised up from a growth of 0.9% in our previous publication) and a fall of 0.6% in June 2026 (revised down from a fall of 0.5% in our previous publication).   The largest positive contribution in August 2026 came from a growth of 5.1% in manufacture of basic pharmaceutical products and pharmaceutical preparations, following an unrevised growth of 3.4% in July 2026. The next largest positive contribution came from a growth of 1.8% in manufacture of transport equipment, but this follows a fall of 1.0% in July 2026 (revised down from a fall of 0.5% in our previous publication). These growths were partially offset by falls in other manufacturing and repair (down 2.1%) and manufacture of food products, beverages and tobacco (down 1.0%). Our Monthly Business Survey (MBS) is used for 74.5% of the production sector by industry weight. The turnover response rate for the MBS element of the production sector was 90.4% in August 2026, which is broadly in line with expected response rates. We would expect this to increase over time as more responses from businesses are received. Any new data will be included in future monthly GDP releases, in line with our National Accounts Revisions Policy . For context, the average turnover response rates for the production sector in 2024 and 2025 now stand at 97.8% and 98.0%, respectively.  More detailed breakdowns on services are available in our Index of Production, UK: August 2026 release .

Construction output is estimated to have decreased by 1.0% in the three months to August 2026 compared with the three months to May 2026. Both new work and repair and maintenance fell during the period, decreasing by 1.4% and 0.3%, respectively. Within new work, the largest negative contribution came from private housing new work, which fell by 3.2%. In repair and maintenance, the largest negative contribution came from non-housing repair and maintenance, which fell by 1.9%. Figure 10: Construction output fell by 1.0% in the three months to August 2026, compared with the three months to May 2026 Monthly index and three-month on three-month growth rates for the construction sector, Great Britain, January 2024 to August 2026

The embedded visualisation below may not display correctly without JavaScript enabled. View it in full screen .

Monthly construction output is estimated to have decreased by 0.2% in August 2026. This is the fourth consecutive decrease in the monthly series, which includes a decrease of 0.5% in July 2026 (revised from an increase of 0.1%), and a decrease of 0.3% (revised from a decrease of 0.1%) in June 2026. The decrease in monthly output in August 2026 came solely from a decrease in new work, which fell by 0.7%, while repair and maintenance grew by 0.4%. At the sector level, the main contribution to the monthly decrease in new work was private housing new work, which fell by 1.9%.
